title: Sufficient Invariant Learning for Distribution Shift

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant vision problem: maintaining worst-group accuracy under spurious correlations and distribution shifts. SGDRO offers a simple, architecture-independent combination of an average-loss SAM perturbation and group-DRO updates. Algorithm 1 makes the main implementation understandable.

The Waterbirds evaluation includes ERM, SAM, and GDRO over five seeds. Under the same weight decay, SGDRO improves worst-group accuracy over GDRO from 86.5% to 87.2% and group-average accuracy from 90.4% to 90.6%, with improvements in both minority groups.

The groupwise curvature measurements provide useful evidence beyond accuracy. In Table 2, SGDRO reduces both leading Hessian eigenvalues in every group relative to GDRO; the largest overall eigenvalue decreases from 356.6 to 268.7.

Evaluation extends to six DomainBed datasets with training-domain validation and three seeds. The average accuracy of 71.4%, versus 70.1% for GDRO and 70.9% for ERM, provides evidence of potential usefulness beyond Waterbirds. Achieving the highest benchmark average is not necessary for this contribution to have value.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are unsupported. Section 3.1 writes the Taylor expansion using overall-loss derivatives, although Equation 3 requires the selected group's gradient and Hessian: approximately ∇L_g + ρH_g∇L_S/||∇L_S|| for a fixed active group. Correcting these indices would still provide only a local update interpretation, not a guarantee of common flat minima or worst-group generalization. An ascent direction for the average loss need not increase the worst-group loss, and the manuscript supplies no argument resolving this issue.

The distinctive design choice is not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison against applying SAM directly to the group-DRO objective, using group-specific perturbations, or updating group weights using unperturbed losses. SAM is also absent from the DomainBed comparison. Consequently, the evidence does not establish the advantage of the proposed average-loss perturbation over other straightforward combinations of the two existing methods.

The claimed reduction of the accuracy trade-off is not demonstrated by Table 1. Relative to GDRO, the 0.7-point worst-group improvement accompanies a decrease in weighted average accuracy from 93.8% to 93.1%, and both majority-group accuracies decline. The five-seed evaluation is valuable, but Table 1 does not define its error bars or quantify uncertainty in the improvement. The results support a modest alternative trade-off more clearly than the claimed significant improvement with alleviated majority-group degradation.

The curvature findings are overinterpreted. Lower test-loss Hessian eigenvalues demonstrate lower measured local curvature, but do not establish shared group minima, reduced generalization gaps, or reliance on essential features. SGDRO is also not uniformly flatter than all baselines: the LL group's largest eigenvalue is 265.2, compared with SAM's 90.2. Comparisons with ERM/SAM additionally change weight decay from 0.0001 to 1.0, limiting attribution, although the GDRO/SGDRO comparison controls this factor.

Reproducibility is only partially supported by pseudocode and references to baseline settings. The DomainBed search range for the new radius parameter, concrete backbone configuration, and minibatch/group-sampling procedure are not specified, and no code link is provided. These reporting issues are secondary to the deciding concerns: the useful empirical signal does not sufficiently establish the distinctive mechanism or support the central theoretical claims, so the balance favors weak rejection.
